title: 12 Controls That Keep an AI Agent From Wiping Your Production Database
subtitle: For CTOs and ops leaders at 10-200 person SaaS companies: the 12 controls to run before an AI agent touches production, so a stray token can't delete your data in 9 seconds.

sections.title: Credential & Permission Scoping
sections.description: Most agent disasters start with a token that was never scoped to what the agent actually needs.

items.text: Issue a dedicated agent identity per environment
items.tip: One agent, one IAM role, one revocable key. If you can't kill it from a single console in under 30 seconds, it's wrong. Never let an agent inherit a developer's token or CI service account.

items.text: Scope every token to the narrowest resource and action set
items.tip: Read-only by default. Write access only on the specific tables, buckets, or queues the agent touches. The PocketOS agent found a blanket Railway CLI token; scoped to staging, the database would still exist.

items.text: Block destructive verbs at the IAM layer, not in the prompt
items.tip: DELETE, DROP, TRUNCATE, rm -rf, volume:delete should be denied by policy even if the agent calls them. A system prompt that says 'never delete production data' is a request. An IAM deny is a wall.

items.text: Rotate agent credentials on a fixed cadence and on every model upgrade
items.tip: A new model version reasons differently about its tools. Treat each upgrade as a fresh key.

sections.title: Human-in-the-Loop Checkpoints
sections.description: Autonomy is fine until an action can't be undone. Then a human types the confirmation.

items.text: Require explicit confirmation for any action that mutates production state
items.tip: A typed DELETE or APPROVE from a named human, not a click. 'Are you sure?' buttons get rubber-stamped. Forcing the operator to type the resource name forces them to read it.

items.text: Define the irreversibility threshold in writing and publish the list
items.tip: Any action a junior engineer can't undo in under 5 minutes needs human approval. Write the list down so it isn't decided in the moment.

items.text: Route 15-20% of edge cases to a human queue by design
items.tip: A 100% autonomous rate means your scope is too narrow or your guardrails are off. A review queue isn't the agent failing. It's the agent working correctly.

sections.title: Backup & Recovery Isolation
sections.description: If the agent can reach production, it must not be able to reach what restores production.

items.text: Store backups on a separate volume, account, and credential scope from production
items.tip: PocketOS lost its backups because they sat on the same Railway volume the agent deleted. Cross-account backups would have saved the company.

items.text: Test restore from backup monthly with a real recovery drill
items.tip: Untested backups are theatre. Time the drill and write down who can run it when you're asleep.

items.text: Maintain point-in-time recovery on the database itself, not just nightly snapshots
items.tip: Supabase and most managed Postgres offer PITR. A nightly snapshot still loses you a full day of customer data.

sections.title: Action Logging & Anomaly Detection
sections.description: You can't investigate what the agent did if the agent could rewrite the record of it.

items.text: Log every agent action with timestamp, tool call, arguments, and outcome to an append-only store the agent cannot write to
items.tip: The PocketOS agent admitted what it did, but that only helped because the logs survived. Put logs somewhere the agent holds no credentials for.

items.text: Alert on any first-time tool call, any call to a new resource, or any burst above 3x normal volume
items.tip: An agent that has never touched the production volume suddenly issuing a delete against it is the alert. Catch the novelty, not just the failure.

sections.title: Scope & Blast Radius Controls
sections.description: Decide in advance how much a single bad decision is allowed to cost you.

items.text: Constrain the agent to a single environment per deployment
items.tip: One agent for staging. A separately credentialed agent for production. They share no keys, no env vars, no shell.

items.text: Wrap every tool the agent can call in a thin adapter that enforces scope, irreversibility checks, logging, and rate limits
items.tip: This is the single most useful pattern. The agent talks to your wrappers, never to raw SDKs or CLIs. It turns 'trust the model' into 'trust the wrapper.'
